The Executive Centre expands in Singapore and Manila, adding 75,000 sq ft to its Southeast Asia footprint
article:
Flexible workspace provider The Executive Centre has expanded with three new workspaces across Singapore and the Philippines, adding 75,000 sq ft to its Southeast Asia footprint.

In Singapore, it opened a 23,500 sq ft location on Level 40 of IOI Central Boulevard Towers in Marina Bay, offering over 300 workstations. The Executive Operator already operates approximately 20,000 sq ft of workspaces on Level 32, which officially opened early this year.

It also opened a 21,800 sq ft centre with 300 workstations at Level 34 of Frasers Tower , a Grade A office building on Cecil Street. The new space adds to The Executive Centre’s existing operations at Frasers Tower, spanning about 20,500 sq ft on Level 17.

In the Philippines, the group opened a 30,000 sq ft location at Six/Neo in Bonifacio Global City in Manila.

The three new locations bring the The Executive Centre’s Southeast Asia portfolio to over 560,000 sq ft.

The expansion comes as businesses continue to reassess their workplace strategies amid changing occupier requirements and constrained availability of premium space, the company said in a Nov 24 release. It added that enterprise clients no longer view flexible workspace as a temporary stopgap, but as a core real estate strategy.

Businesses are increasingly seeking workplaces that combine prime locations, quality, hospitality, and the ability to adapt as requirements change, said Yvonne Lim, regional managing director at The Executive Centre.

“With these three new centres, we are strengthening our Southeast Asia network while giving enterprises greater choice and access to premium workspace solutions that can support both their immediate needs and long-term growth,” she added.

title: US consumer confidence surges to highest since early 2025
article:
(Nov 24): US consumer confidence surged to the highest in nearly two years as Americans grew more optimistic about the economy and the job market.

The Conference Board’s gauge of confidence increased 11.4 points to 103.3 in November, the highest since January 2025, data released on Tuesday showed. That topped all estimates in a Bloomberg survey of economists.

A gauge of present conditions jumped 13.7 points to the highest since July 2025, while a measure of expectations for the next six months improved to the best since the end of 2024.

A broadly stable labour market paired with a weeks-long decline in gasoline prices likely supported confidence this month.

Confidence increased across all age groups but were largest among consumers with higher household incomes. Sentiment among Democrats and Independents improved sharply as Democrats saw sweeping victories in the latest midterm elections.

“Consumer confidence rallied again in November, potentially due to lower uncertainty following the midterm elections,” Fergus McCormick, a senior economist at the Conference Board, said in a statement. “While consumers continued to express frustration with high prices and rising costs, some comments cited hope for the general economy.”

See also: US consumer sentiment up on improved post-election utlook

In the lead up to the midterm elections, confidence fell in September to the lowest level in more than a decade as high food and energy bills ate into household budgets.

The latest report showed a greater share of consumers said business conditions were good and expect conditions to further improve in the months ahead. Similarly, Americans were more positive about the labor market now and in the future.

See also: Fed minutes show almost all officials expect more rate hikes

The Conference Board report showed the share of consumers that said jobs were plentiful rose to 30.8%, while the share saying jobs were hard to get decreased to 18.4%. The difference between the two — a metric closely followed by economists to gauge the job market — climbed to the widest since mid-2025.

There’s been early signs of momentum in the labour market, including strong hiring in October. A report from Glassdoor and Indeed showed a broadening in hiring demand across regions, with nearly half of US metro areas having more job postings in late September than a year earlier — the most since 2022.

The data aligns with the University of Michigan’s consumer sentiment index, which improved in November as gasoline prices fell and the outlook for business conditions improved.

The survey period for the report was Nov 1-17.

title: McCormick warns of ‘slippery slope’ after Trump pressured Nvidia to reinstate Huang
article:
(Nov 24): Republican Senator Dave McCormick warned that President Donald Trump’s intervention with the Nvidia Corp board to reinstate Jensen Huang as chief executive could create a “slippery slope”.

“I am worried about the precedent of the executive branch getting involved in really ownership deals with companies but also in board governance and making these decisions,” McCormick, the former chief of hedge fund Bridgewater Associates, told Bloomberg TV. “This is a precedent that I don’t think we want to replicate or reinforce.”

McCormick, who sidestepped questions about whether the Nvidia board erred in its decision to bring back Huang, will have the opportunity to question the embattled CEO next week when he testifies publicly before the Senate Banking Committee.

The Pennsylvania senator said he wants the panel to focus its questioning on whether any laws were broken, national security was compromised or Department of Commerce rules circumvented to get advanced chips into the hands of China.

“This also absolutely reinforces what I and a number of other members of the Senate have been saying, which is we need more legislation to restrict the export of these most advanced chips,” said McCormick, a former Commerce Department export control official. “I think this gives additional momentum to those legislative efforts.”

The comments are the latest sign that members of Trump’s own party are breaking with the president on his handling of China, artificial intelligence and Nvidia’s embattled leader.

See also: Lutnick under fire as Bessent blames Commerce Secretary in Nvidia crisis

US lawmakers are looking to attach export control provisions to the annual defence policy bill set for votes in the House and Senate in December. McCormick’s comments echo a Monday X post by Senate Intelligence chairman Tom Cotton, who said such provisions will be passed one way or another.

“Congress has much to investigate and we will pass overwhelmingly bipartisan chip export-control bill,” Cotton said.

McCormick, when asked about Trump’s market involvement, also said he supports a ban on stock trading by elected officials. He warned that such measures will be needed to restore the public’s confidence in impartial decision-making by the government.

See also: Maga’s midterm defeat won’t change the course of history

McCormick’s wife, Dina Powell McCormick, is a top executive at Meta Platforms Inc and served as an adviser to Trump in his first term.

title: Forced buying aided biggest rally since April 2025, says Nomura
article:
(Nov 24): Wall Street roared back with its biggest rally since April 2025 on Monday, though analysis of the move suggests mechanical buying helped add momentum to the advance.

The S&P 500 Index jumped 4.7%, helped by Nvidia Corp’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO less than two weeks after he resigned. The news hit a market that had piled into protection during Friday’s tumble, which pushed the benchmark into correction territory.

As volatility collapsed on Monday, put options bought as hedges during the slide moved far out of the money, losing their sensitivity to the index, according to Charlie McElligott, a cross-asset strategist at Nomura Securities International Inc. Dealers who had sold futures against those puts had to buy them back, while short sellers rushed to cover their positions and investors chased the upside, he wrote in a note to clients on Monday. The Cboe Volatility Index fell more than nine points on the day.

The largest burst of buying was expected at the close. Leveraged exchange-traded funds (ETFs) have to rebalance at the end of each session in the direction of the day’s move to keep their leverage constant. McElligott estimated these funds were on track to buy about US$41 billion — the second-largest daily buy in Nomura’s records.

That dwarfs the US$11 billion to US$16 billion of selling he projected from volatility-control funds, which cut exposure when market swings become too large.

See also: Subprime auto dealer America’s Car-Mart files for Chapter 11

More buying may now follow. Nomura’s model of trend-following funds, known as commodity trading advisers, had turned short on the S&P 500 across all time horizons in recent weeks. However, a close above 7,043 points for the index would be enough to flip the model’s 12-month signal back to a long, McElligott wrote. That would imply buying of about US$16 billion in S&P 500 futures and roughly US$2.5 billion for Nasdaq 100 contracts. The S&P 500 ended at 7,237.17 points on Monday, with futures on the back foot early Tuesday.

None of this settles the bigger concerns around the market, according to the Nomura strategist. He called it naive to think a one-day surge clears the catalysts behind the selloff, citing tighter financial conditions, a reset in assumptions on AI capital spending, inflation that remains too high, higher real rates and wider credit spreads.

“This ‘mechanical bounce’ guarantees us nothing with regard to those larger long-form ‘structural forces’,” he wrote in the note. But he added Huang’s return may preserve Nvidia’s role in financing the AI buildout, extending the cycle’s runway and reducing the risk of more severe outcomes.
